items.stem: Which company began delivering blood supplies by drone in Rwanda in 2016?
options: Zipline
Wing
Amazon Prime Air
DJI
items.answer: Zipline
items.markingKey: A. Drones deliver to rural clinics, reducing delivery times from hours to minutes.

items.stem: Diego writes: "Leapfrogging means older infrastructure is never needed." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Mobile networks still need electricity, backhaul fibre and regulation; leapfrogging skips some stages but depends on other infrastructure.
items.markingKey: Mobile networks still need electricity, backhaul fibre and regulation; leapfrogging skips some stages but depends on other infrastructure. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): The SDGs were adopted in 2015.
Reason (R): The SDGs replaced the Millennium Development Goals.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: B. Both true, but replacing the MDGs does not explain the year of adoption.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Digital technologies can accelerate progress on the SDGs, but they can also widen existing divides."
— Paraphrase of a common theme in UN Secretary-General reports on digital cooperation

Explain one way digital technologies could widen existing divides.
items.answer: Services moving online (banking, government, education) disadvantage people without access or skills, so those already marginalised lose out further.
items.markingKey: Services moving online (banking, government, education) disadvantage people without access or skills, so those already marginalised lose out further. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: In a low-income country with a population of 8 million, the share of people using the internet rose from 19% to 35% over 8 years (assume the population is constant). Calculate (i) the change in percentage points, (ii) the percentage increase, and (iii) the number of additional internet users. Explain why this growth alone does not show progress towards SDG 4 (quality education).
items.answer: (i) 16 percentage points; (ii) 84.2%; (iii) 1.28 million people; access is not the same as meaningful use – affordability, device quality, digital skills, relevant content and who gained access (gender, rural/urban) all matter
items.markingKey: (i) 35 − 19 = 16 pp [A1]; (ii) 16 ÷ 19 × 100 = 84.2% [M1 A1]; (iii) 8 m × 16% = 1.28 million [A1]. Access ≠ meaningful use / learning outcomes; distribution across groups unknown [R1 R1].

items.stem: Briefly describe Digital Green in India and explain what it reveals about media and networks supporting SDG 2.
items.answer: Digital Green, which grew out of a Microsoft Research project, produces short videos of local farmers demonstrating techniques, shown in villages to share agricultural knowledge. Locally made content proved more trusted and cost-effective than traditional extension visits.
items.markingKey: Context (Digital Green, which grew out of a Microsoft Research project, produces short videos of local farmers demonstrating techniques, shown in villages to share agricultural knowledge.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: locally made content proved more trusted and cost-effective than traditional extension visits. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to media and networks supporting SDG 2.

items.stem: Evaluate the extent to which digital technologies help achieve one Sustainable Development Goal.
items.answer: Choose an SDG; real examples (M-Pesa, Zipline, Digital Green); opportunities vs risks (inequality, environment, dependency); stakeholders; concepts (change, power, values); judgement.
items.markingKey: Choose an SDG; real examples (M-Pesa, Zipline, Digital Green); opportunities vs risks (inequality, environment, dependency); stakeholders; concepts (change, power, values); judgement.

items.stem: "Digital technologies are essential for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Digital technologies are an important enabler but not sufficient; their benefits depend on inclusive access and sustainable design.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: mobile money, telemedicine, e-learning and precision agriculture show measurable gains; data improves monitoring of SDG progress. Arguments against: environmental costs of devices and data centres; unequal access widens divides; many goals depend more on governance, funding and infrastructure. Supported judgement: Digital technologies are an important enabler but not sufficient; their benefits depend on inclusive access and sustainable design. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: Explain how mobile money can contribute to SDG 1 (no poverty).
items.answer: It gives unbanked people a safe way to save, receive remittances and pay, smoothing income shocks and enabling small businesses; studies of M-Pesa found reductions in poverty, especially for women-headed households.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It gives unbanked people a safe way to save, receive remittances and pay, smoothing income shocks and enabling small businesses; studies of M-Pesa found reductions in poverty, especially for women-headed households. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why the environmental footprint of digital technology is a risk for SDG 13 (climate action).
items.answer: Manufacturing devices, running data centres and networks, and training AI models consume energy, water and minerals and create e-waste; rapid growth and the rebound effect can outweigh efficiency gains.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Manufacturing devices, running data centres and networks, and training AI models consume energy, water and minerals and create e-waste; rapid growth and the rebound effect can outweigh efficiency gains. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between meaningful connectivity and access to technology.
items.answer: Access means a connection is available; meaningful connectivity means regular use with an adequate device, affordable data, sufficient speed and the skills to benefit.
items.markingKey: Access means a connection is available; meaningful connectivity means regular use with an adequate device, affordable data, sufficient speed and the skills to benefit. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Significantly increase access to information and communications technology and strive to provide universal and affordable access to the Internet in least developed countries by 2020."
— UN Sustainable Development Goals, Target 9.c (2015)

With reference to the source, explain why this target was not achieved.
items.answer: Universal, affordable access in least developed countries was not reached by 2020 because of infrastructure costs, high data and device prices relative to income, low digital skills and limited electricity.
items.markingKey: Universal, affordable access in least developed countries was not reached by 2020 because of infrastructure costs, high data and device prices relative to income, low digital skills and limited electricity. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: "The benefits of digital technology for development outweigh its environmental costs." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Benefits can outweigh costs only with circular design, renewable energy and fair e-waste policies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: efficiency gains (smart grids, dematerialisation); improved health and incomes. Arguments against: e-waste and energy growth; rebound effects; costs fall on poorer countries (e-waste dumping, mining). Supported judgement: Benefits can outweigh costs only with circular design, renewable energy and fair e-waste policies. Markbands (8 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that the benefits of digital technology for development outweigh its environmental costs.
items.answer: Benefits can outweigh costs only with circular design, renewable energy and fair e-waste policies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: efficiency gains (smart grids, dematerialisation); improved health and incomes. Arguments against: e-waste and energy growth; rebound effects; costs fall on poorer countries (e-waste dumping, mining). Supported judgement: Benefits can outweigh costs only with circular design, renewable energy and fair e-waste policies. items.stem: From the end of 2024, which connector did the EU require on new mobile phones sold in the EU?
options: USB-C
Micro-USB
Mini-USB
Lightning
items.answer: USB-C
items.markingKey: A. The common-charger directive aims to reduce e-waste and inconvenience.

items.stem: Distinguish between recycling and repair and reuse.
items.answer: Recycling recovers materials after a device is discarded but loses embodied energy; repair and reuse extend the life of the whole device and avoid new manufacturing, so they are higher in the waste hierarchy.
items.markingKey: Recycling recovers materials after a device is discarded but loses embodied energy; repair and reuse extend the life of the whole device and avoid new manufacturing, so they are higher in the waste hierarchy. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why AI growth is raising concerns about data-centre sustainability.
items.answer: Training and running large AI models needs large amounts of electricity and water for cooling, and rapid expansion of data centres can strain grids and delay climate targets. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Training and running large AI models needs large amounts of electricity and water for cooling, and rapid expansion of data centres can strain grids and delay climate targets. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Only 22.3% of the year's e-waste mass was documented as having been properly collected and recycled."
— Global E-waste Monitor 2024 (UNITAR and ITU)

With reference to the source, explain one consequence of the low collection rate.
items.answer: Most e-waste ends up in landfill, incineration or informal recycling, losing valuable materials and releasing hazardous substances that harm health and the environment.
items.markingKey: Most e-waste ends up in landfill, incineration or informal recycling, losing valuable materials and releasing hazardous substances that harm health and the environment. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: A student claims: "Digital services are "weightless" and have no environmental impact." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Streaming, cloud storage and AI rely on physical data centres, networks and devices that use energy, water and raw materials.
items.markingKey: Streaming, cloud storage and AI rely on physical data centres, networks and devices that use energy, water and raw materials. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Evaluate the effectiveness of one intervention designed to make computing more sustainable.
items.answer: E.g. EU common charger, right-to-repair, EPR, renewable-powered data centres, Ethereum's Merge; aims; evidence; stakeholders (manufacturers, consumers, recyclers, workers); limitations; judgement.
items.markingKey: E.g. EU common charger, right-to-repair, EPR, renewable-powered data centres, Ethereum's Merge; aims; evidence; stakeholders (manufacturers, consumers, recyclers, workers); limitations; judgement.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "embodied emissions".
items.answer: The greenhouse gases released in mining materials, manufacturing and transporting a device before it is used
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the greenhouse gases released in mining materials, manufacturing and transporting a device before it is used. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the manufacturing stage matters for the carbon footprint of a smartphone.
items.answer: Most of a smartphone's lifetime emissions come from mining materials and manufacturing (embodied emissions), so keeping devices longer through repair and reuse saves more than reducing charging energy.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Most of a smartphone's lifetime emissions come from mining materials and manufacturing (embodied emissions), so keeping devices longer through repair and reuse saves more than reducing charging energy. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to Agbogbloshie, Ghana, explain how it illustrates global inequality in e-waste.
items.answer: For years a site in Accra known for informal e-waste processing, where workers burned cables to recover copper, exposing themselves and residents to toxic fumes; the site was cleared by authorities in 2021. The costs of e-waste fall heavily on poor workers in the Global South, showing the need for EPR and fair recycling.
items.markingKey: Context (For years a site in Accra known for informal e-waste processing, where workers burned cables to recover copper, exposing themselves and residents to toxic fumes; the site was cleared by authorities in 2021.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the costs of e-waste fall heavily on poor workers in the Global South, showing the need for EPR and fair recycling. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to global inequality in e-waste.

items.stem: A data centre's IT equipment uses 80 GWh of electricity a year. Its power usage effectiveness (PUE) is 1.4. Calculate (i) the total facility energy use, (ii) the energy used for cooling and other overheads, and (iii) the saving if PUE is improved to 1.2.
items.answer: (i) 112 GWh; (ii) 32 GWh; (iii) 16 GWh per year
items.markingKey: PUE = total ÷ IT, so total = 80 × 1.4 = 112 GWh [M1 A1]; overhead = 112 − 80 = 32 GWh [A1]; saving = 80 × (1.4 − 1.2) = 16 GWh [A1].

items.stem: With reference to two real-world examples, discuss the claim that technology companies should be required to report the environmental impact of their AI services.
items.answer: Standardised mandatory reporting is justified as a first step towards regulating AI's environmental footprint.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: transparency enables accountability and comparison; informs users and regulators. Arguments against: measurement is complex (embodied vs operational); compliance costs; risk of greenwashing. Supported judgement: Standardised mandatory reporting is justified as a first step towards regulating AI's environmental footprint. Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "digital inclusion".
items.answer: Ensuring that all individuals and communities have the access, devices, affordability and skills needed to use digital technologies meaningfully
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: ensuring that all individuals and communities have the access, devices, affordability and skills needed to use digital technologies meaningfully. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between a demand-side intervention and a supply-side intervention.
items.answer: Supply-side interventions build infrastructure or lower prices (fibre, satellites, community Wi-Fi); demand-side interventions build skills, relevance and confidence to use technology (digital literacy training).
items.markingKey: Supply-side interventions build infrastructure or lower prices (fibre, satellites, community Wi-Fi); demand-side interventions build skills, relevance and confidence to use technology (digital literacy training). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why providing devices alone often fails to improve learning.
items.answer: Without teacher training, relevant content, maintenance, electricity and connectivity, devices are underused; OLPC evaluations in Peru found little impact on test scores. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Without teacher training, relevant content, maintenance, electricity and connectivity, devices are underused; OLPC evaluations in Peru found little impact on test scores. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Free Basics is not the internet. It is Facebook deciding what the poor can see."
— Paraphrase of arguments made by the Save the Internet campaign in India, 2015

Explain the concern expressed in the source.
items.answer: A single company acting as gatekeeper controls which services users can reach, limiting choice and competition and violating net neutrality.
items.markingKey: A single company acting as gatekeeper controls which services users can reach, limiting choice and competition and violating net neutrality. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Felix writes: "Digital inclusion is only a problem in low-income countries." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Older people, low-income households, disabled people and rural communities in wealthy countries also face exclusion.
items.markingKey: Older people, low-income households, disabled people and rural communities in wealthy countries also face exclusion. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Evaluate one intervention designed to improve digital inclusion.
items.answer: E.g. Giga, Free Basics, OLPC, community networks, India's PMGDISHA digital-literacy programme; aims; stakeholders; supply vs demand side; evidence; limitations; recommendation.
items.markingKey: E.g. Giga, Free Basics, OLPC, community networks, India's PMGDISHA digital-literacy programme; aims; stakeholders; supply vs demand side; evidence; limitations; recommendation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "community network"?
options: The use of information and communication technologies to support social and economic development, especially in low- and middle-income countries
A fund, usually paid into by telecom operators, used to extend connectivity to areas that are not commercially profitable
Laws or principles requiring manufacturers to make spare parts, tools and repair information available so that devices can be repaired
A locally owned and operated communications network built by a community to meet its own connectivity needs
items.answer: A locally owned and operated communications network built by a community to meet its own connectivity needs
items.markingKey: D. "community network" is a locally owned and operated communications network built by a community to meet its own connectivity needs.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Free Basics and Giga.
items.answer: Free Basics (Meta) offered zero-rated access to selected services through operators, raising net-neutrality concerns; Giga (UNICEF–ITU) aims to connect schools to the open internet with public and private financing.
items.markingKey: Free Basics (Meta) offered zero-rated access to selected services through operators, raising net-neutrality concerns; Giga (UNICEF–ITU) aims to connect schools to the open internet with public and private financing. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In a country, average income (GNI per capita) is US$3,600 a year and 1 GB of mobile data costs US$3. The UN Broadband Commission target is that 1 GB should cost no more than 2% of average monthly income. Calculate the cost of 1 GB as a percentage of average monthly income and state whether the target is met.
items.answer: 1%; target met
items.markingKey: Monthly income = 3,600 ÷ 12 = 300 [M1]; 3 ÷ 300 × 100 = 1% [A1]; ≤ 2% so target met [A1].

items.stem: Using Free Basics in India (2015–16) as an example, explain net neutrality and power in digital inclusion.
items.answer: Facebook's zero-rated app offering free access to selected services was opposed by the Save the Internet campaign; TRAI ruled against discriminatory data pricing in February 2016. The case showed that inclusion interventions controlled by one company can conflict with users' rights and an open internet.
items.markingKey: Context (Facebook's zero-rated app offering free access to selected services was opposed by the Save the Internet campaign; TRAI ruled against discriminatory data pricing in February 2016.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the case showed that inclusion interventions controlled by one company can conflict with users' rights and an open internet. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to net neutrality and power in digital inclusion.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "leapfrogging"?
options: Ensuring that all individuals and communities have the access, devices, affordability and skills needed to use digital technologies meaningfully
When efficiency gains from technology lower costs and so increase overall use, cancelling out some of the expected environmental savings
Skipping an older stage of technology, such as moving straight to mobile phones and mobile money without building landline and bank-branch networks
A fund, usually paid into by telecom operators, used to extend connectivity to areas that are not commercially profitable
items.answer: Skipping an older stage of technology, such as moving straight to mobile phones and mobile money without building landline and bank-branch networks
items.markingKey: C. "leapfrogging" is skipping an older stage of technology, such as moving straight to mobile phones and mobile money without building landline and bank-branch networks.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An economic model that keeps products and materials in use through repair, reuse, refurbishment and recycling rather than "take, make, dispose""?
options: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
power usage effectiveness (PUE)
circular economy
leapfrogging
items.answer: circular economy
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of circular economy.

items.stem: Which UNICEF and ITU initiative, launched in 2019, aims to connect every school in the world to the internet?
items.answer: Giga
items.markingKey: Giga. It maps schools and works with governments and companies on financing.

items.stem: "Leapfrogging means older infrastructure is never needed." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Mobile networks still need electricity, backhaul fibre and regulation; leapfrogging skips some stages but depends on other infrastructure.
items.markingKey: Mobile networks still need electricity, backhaul fibre and regulation; leapfrogging skips some stages but depends on other infrastructure. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between carbon intensity and PUE.
items.answer: PUE measures how much extra energy a data centre uses beyond its IT load; carbon intensity measures how much CO2 is emitted per unit of electricity, which depends on the energy source.
items.markingKey: PUE measures how much extra energy a data centre uses beyond its IT load; carbon intensity measures how much CO2 is emitted per unit of electricity, which depends on the energy source. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Tomás writes: "Once an area has network coverage, everyone in it is connected." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Coverage does not mean use – the "usage gap" is caused by device costs, data prices, lack of skills, relevance and social barriers.
items.markingKey: Coverage does not mean use – the "usage gap" is caused by device costs, data prices, lack of skills, relevance and social barriers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a risk and an opportunity of digital technology for the SDGs.
items.answer: Opportunities include mobile money, telemedicine and precision agriculture; risks include e-waste, energy use, surveillance and widening digital divides.
items.markingKey: Opportunities include mobile money, telemedicine and precision agriculture; risks include e-waste, energy use, surveillance and widening digital divides. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why e-waste is a global justice issue.
items.answer: Much e-waste is exported or informally processed in poorer countries, where workers, often without protection, burn or dismantle devices and are exposed to toxic substances, while the benefits of the devices were enjoyed elsewhere.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Much e-waste is exported or informally processed in poorer countries, where workers, often without protection, burn or dismantle devices and are exposed to toxic substances, while the benefits of the devices were enjoyed elsewhere. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A country of 2 million people generates 120 thousand tonnes of e-waste a year, of which 22% is formally collected and recycled. Calculate (i) the tonnes formally recycled, (ii) the tonnes not formally recycled, and (iii) the e-waste generated per person in kg. Suggest one intervention to raise the collection rate and explain how it would work.
items.answer: (i) 26.4 thousand tonnes; (ii) 93.6 thousand tonnes; (iii) 60 kg per person; e.g. extended producer responsibility (EPR) making manufacturers fund take-back; deposit-return schemes; convenient collection points
items.markingKey: (i) 120 × 22% = 26.4 kt [A1]; (ii) 120 − 26.4 = 93.6 kt [A1]; (iii) 120,000 t × 1000 kg ÷ 2,000,000 = 60 kg [M1 A1]. Named intervention [R1]; mechanism (incentive/responsibility/convenience) [R1].

items.stem: Two digital-inclusion projects are compared. Project A (community Wi-Fi hubs) cost US$12 million and connected 80,000 people. Project B (subsidised smartphones with digital-skills training) cost US$1 million and connected 20,000 people. Calculate the cost per person connected for each project and identify the more cost-effective project.
items.answer: A US$150 per person; B US$50 per person; Project B is more cost-effective

items.stem: In a low-income country with a population of 60 million, the share of people using the internet rose from 39% to 81% over 4 years (assume the population is constant). Calculate (i) the change in percentage points, (ii) the percentage increase, and (iii) the number of additional internet users. Read the source below.

"Fair materials, longer-lasting products and repairable design are at the heart of what we do."
— Paraphrase of Fairphone's stated mission

items.answer: Modular, repairable phones remain a small niche with higher prices; system-wide change needs regulation such as right-to-repair laws.
items.markingKey: Modular, repairable phones remain a small niche with higher prices; system-wide change needs regulation such as right-to-repair laws. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

"Connecting every school to the Internet and every young person to information, opportunity and choice."
— Stated mission of Giga, UNICEF and ITU

items.answer: Many schools lack electricity and are far from fibre backbones, so connections are costly to build and maintain; ongoing funding for data and devices is also needed.

items.stem: In a low-income country with a population of 40 million, the share of people using the internet rose from 32% to 63% over 8 years (assume the population is constant). Calculate (i) the change in percentage points, (ii) the percentage increase, and (iii) the number of additional internet users. Explain why this growth alone does not show progress towards SDG 4 (quality education).
items.answer: (i) 31 percentage points; (ii) 96.9%; (iii) 12.4 million people; access is not the same as meaningful use – affordability, device quality, digital skills, relevant content and who gained access (gender, rural/urban) all matter

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Right-to-repair laws are the most effective way to reduce e-waste."
items.answer: Right-to-repair is highly effective when combined with longer software support, EPR and consumer incentives.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: extend device life, avoiding embodied emissions; EU Right to Repair Directive (2024) and ecodesign rules on spare parts. Arguments against: consumers may still prefer new devices; software updates and design matter too; collection and EPR needed for end-of-life devices. Supported judgement: Right-to-repair is highly effective when combined with longer software support, EPR and consumer incentives.

items.stem: "Building infrastructure is more important than teaching digital literacy for digital inclusion." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Both are necessary; demand-side interventions are often the missing piece where coverage already exists.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: without connectivity, skills cannot be used; billions remain offline. Arguments against: the usage gap is larger than the coverage gap; skills determine safe and meaningful use; OLPC shows hardware alone fails. Supported judgement: Both are necessary; demand-side interventions are often the missing piece where coverage already exists. items.stem: "The benefits of digital technology for development outweigh its environmental costs." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Benefits can outweigh costs only with circular design, renewable energy and fair e-waste policies.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: efficiency gains (smart grids, dematerialisation); improved health and incomes. Arguments against: e-waste and energy growth; rebound effects; costs fall on poorer countries (e-waste dumping, mining). Supported judgement: Benefits can outweigh costs only with circular design, renewable energy and fair e-waste policies. Markbands [8]: 7–8 – well-developed evaluation of impacts/implications, specific real-world example(s), balanced and with a supported conclusion; 5–6 – evaluation with relevant example(s) but uneven balance; 3–4 – some relevant points, mainly descriptive, conclusion asserted; 1–2 – limited, general response.

items.stem: "Right-to-repair laws are the most effective way to reduce e-waste." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Right-to-repair is highly effective when combined with longer software support, EPR and consumer incentives.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: extend device life, avoiding embodied emissions; EU Right to Repair Directive (2024) and ecodesign rules on spare parts. Arguments against: consumers may still prefer new devices; software updates and design matter too; collection and EPR needed for end-of-life devices. Supported judgement: Right-to-repair is highly effective when combined with longer software support, EPR and consumer incentives. Markbands (12 marks): Markbands (five bands, scaled to the marks available): top – focused on the question; accurate use of Digital Society concepts, content and contexts; specific, well-explained real-world examples; balanced analysis of impacts and implications for different stakeholders; a clear, well-supported conclusion. Upper-middle – relevant examples and some balance; conclusion reasoned. Middle – some relevant knowledge, partly descriptive; conclusion stated. Lower – limited, general knowledge, mainly descriptive. Bottom – minimal relevant material.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "When efficiency gains from technology lower costs and so increase overall use, cancelling out some of the expected environmental savings"?
options: e-waste
community network
rebound effect
circular economy
items.answer: rebound effect
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of rebound effect.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "e-waste"?
options: Discarded electrical and electronic equipment, which contains valuable metals and hazardous substances such as lead and mercury
Skipping an older stage of technology, such as moving straight to mobile phones and mobile money without building landline and bank-branch networks
A locally owned and operated communications network built by a community to meet its own connectivity needs
The skills to find, evaluate, create and communicate information safely and effectively using digital technologies
items.answer: Discarded electrical and electronic equipment, which contains valuable metals and hazardous substances such as lead and mercury
items.markingKey: A. "e-waste" is discarded electrical and electronic equipment, which contains valuable metals and hazardous substances such as lead and mercury.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "When a mobile operator does not charge data for using particular apps or services, as in Facebook's Free Basics"?
options: digital literacy
universal service fund
zero-rating
digital inclusion
items.answer: zero-rating
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of zero-rating.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): M-Pesa is often described as an example of leapfrogging.
Reason (R): It allowed many Kenyans to use digital financial services without first having a bank account.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: A. Both true; R explains A – people skipped traditional banking.

items.stem: A student claims: "Recycling solves the e-waste problem." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Only about a fifth of e-waste is formally recycled, some materials cannot be recovered economically, and reducing and reusing devices matters more.
items.markingKey: Only about a fifth of e-waste is formally recycled, some materials cannot be recovered economically, and reducing and reusing devices matters more. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why community networks can be effective in remote areas.
items.answer: Local ownership keeps costs low, builds skills and trust, and meets local needs where commercial operators see no profit, as with Zenzeleni in South Africa.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Local ownership keeps costs low, builds skills and trust, and meets local needs where commercial operators see no profit, as with Zenzeleni in South Africa. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a risk and an opportunity of digital technology for the SDGs.
items.answer: Opportunities include mobile money, telemedicine and precision agriculture; risks include e-waste, energy use, surveillance and widening digital divides.
items.markingKey: Opportunities include mobile money, telemedicine and precision agriculture; risks include e-waste, energy use, surveillance and widening digital divides. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why AI growth is raising concerns about data-centre sustainability.
items.answer: Training and running large AI models needs large amounts of electricity and water for cooling, and rapid expansion of data centres can strain grids and delay climate targets.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Training and running large AI models needs large amounts of electricity and water for cooling, and rapid expansion of data centres can strain grids and delay climate targets. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between Giga and Free Basics.
items.answer: Free Basics (Meta) offered zero-rated access to selected services through operators, raising net-neutrality concerns; Giga (UNICEF–ITU) aims to connect schools to the open internet with public and private financing.
items.markingKey: Free Basics (Meta) offered zero-rated access to selected services through operators, raising net-neutrality concerns; Giga (UNICEF–ITU) aims to connect schools to the open internet with public and private financing. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using M-Pesa in Kenya as an example, explain digital technology supporting SDG 1 and SDG 5.
items.answer: Launched by Safaricom in 2007, M-Pesa allowed people to send money by SMS through agents; a 2016 study by Suri and Jack estimated it lifted about 194,000 households (2%) out of extreme poverty. Mobile money improved financial inclusion, especially for women, by leapfrogging traditional banking.
items.markingKey: Context (Launched by Safaricom in 2007, M-Pesa allowed people to send money by SMS through agents; a 2016 study by Suri and Jack estimated it lifted about 194,000 households (2%) out of extreme poverty.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: mobile money improved financial inclusion, especially for women, by leapfrogging traditional banking. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to digital technology supporting SDG 1 and SDG 5.

items.stem: Briefly describe DeepMind data-centre cooling (2016) and explain what it reveals about AI for energy efficiency.
items.answer: Google reported that DeepMind machine learning reduced the energy used for cooling its data centres by up to 40% by predicting and optimising settings. AI can improve efficiency, though growth in demand may outweigh savings (rebound effect).
items.markingKey: Context (Google reported that DeepMind machine learning reduced the energy used for cooling its data centres by up to 40% by predicting and optimising settings.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: AI can improve efficiency, though growth in demand may outweigh savings (rebound effect). – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to AI for energy efficiency.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Zenzeleni Networks, South Africa shows community-led connectivity.
items.answer: A community-owned internet service provider in the rural Eastern Cape, set up with the University of the Western Cape, offering low-cost Wi-Fi powered by solar energy. Local ownership can make connectivity affordable and sustainable, though scaling up and regulation are challenges.
items.markingKey: Context (A community-owned internet service provider in the rural Eastern Cape, set up with the University of the Western Cape, offering low-cost Wi-Fi powered by solar energy.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: local ownership can make connectivity affordable and sustainable, though scaling up and regulation are challenges. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to community-led connectivity.

items.stem: A student claims: "Leapfrogging means older infrastructure is never needed." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Mobile networks still need electricity, backhaul fibre and regulation; leapfrogging skips some stages but depends on other infrastructure.
items.markingKey: Mobile networks still need electricity, backhaul fibre and regulation; leapfrogging skips some stages but depends on other infrastructure. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A data centre's IT equipment uses 20 GWh of electricity a year. Its power usage effectiveness (PUE) is 1.8. Calculate (i) the total facility energy use, (ii) the energy used for cooling and other overheads, and (iii) the saving if PUE is improved to 1.2.
items.answer: (i) 36 GWh; (ii) 16 GWh; (iii) 12 GWh per year
items.markingKey: PUE = total ÷ IT, so total = 20 × 1.8 = 36 GWh [M1 A1]; overhead = 36 − 20 = 16 GWh [A1]; saving = 20 × (1.8 − 1.2) = 12 GWh [A1].

items.stem: Two digital-inclusion projects are compared. Project A (community Wi-Fi hubs) cost US$12 million and connected 40,000 people. Project B (subsidised smartphones with digital-skills training) cost US$10 million and connected 150,000 people. Calculate the cost per person connected for each project and identify the more cost-effective project.
items.answer: A US$300 per person; B US$66.667 per person; Project B is more cost-effective

items.stem: In a low-income country with a population of 60 million, the share of people using the internet rose from 28% to 45% over 10 years (assume the population is constant). Calculate (i) the change in percentage points, (ii) the percentage increase, and (iii) the number of additional internet users. Explain why this growth alone does not show progress towards SDG 4 (quality education).
items.answer: (i) 17 percentage points; (ii) 60.7%; (iii) 10.2 million people; access is not the same as meaningful use – affordability, device quality, digital skills, relevant content and who gained access (gender, rural/urban) all matter
items.markingKey: (i) 45 − 28 = 17 pp [A1]; (ii) 17 ÷ 28 × 100 = 60.7% [M1 A1]; (iii) 60 m × 17% = 10.2 million [A1]. Access ≠ meaningful use / learning outcomes; distribution across groups unknown [R1 R1].

items.stem: "Private technology companies should lead efforts to connect the unconnected." Discuss.
items.answer: Public–private partnerships with public accountability and open-internet safeguards are preferable.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: capital, technology and speed (satellites); commercial incentive for sustainability. Arguments against: profit motive may exclude unprofitable areas; risk of control and data extraction (Free Basics); Project Loon shut down when not viable. Supported judgement: Public–private partnerships with public accountability and open-internet safeguards are preferable. items.stem: "Digital technologies are essential for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Digital technologies are an important enabler but not sufficient; their benefits depend on inclusive access and sustainable design.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: mobile money, telemedicine, e-learning and precision agriculture show measurable gains; data improves monitoring of SDG progress. Arguments against: environmental costs of devices and data centres; unequal access widens divides; many goals depend more on governance, funding and infrastructure. Supported judgement: Digital technologies are an important enabler but not sufficient; their benefits depend on inclusive access and sustainable design. items.stem: "Technology companies should be required to report the environmental impact of their AI services." How far do you agree? Refer to at least one Digital Society concept in your answer.
items.answer: Standardised mandatory reporting is justified as a first step towards regulating AI's environmental footprint.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: transparency enables accountability and comparison; informs users and regulators. Arguments against: measurement is complex (embodied vs operational); compliance costs; risk of greenwashing. Supported judgement: Standardised mandatory reporting is justified as a first step towards regulating AI's environmental footprint. Markbands [12]: 10–12 – sustained, balanced evaluation that integrates the sources/stimulus with specific own knowledge and Digital Society concepts, and reaches a well-supported conclusion; 7–9 – evaluation with relevant evidence and some balance; 4–6 – some analysis, mostly descriptive or one-sided; 1–3 – limited, general points with little evaluation.
